Welcome and Show-and-Tell: Real-World Devices

Alright everyone, let’s get started! Today, one of our students graciously brought in some actual patterned devices from his research lab, so I am going to pass those around. These are lithography masks. You might remember my somewhat janky homemade mask from a previous lecture with the Los Angeles Dodgers logo on it. What is going around the room right now is the real deal.

As you look at them, you will notice different coatings. On one of them, the reddish-brown part is an iron oxide coating, which is opaque to ultraviolet (UV) light. The transparent regions are where the UV light passes through to create patterns. The other mask has a shiny, silver-colored coating—likely chromium—doing the same job of blocking light where we do not want it. Please handle them carefully, but do not worry too much about fingerprints; they are expendable for our purposes today.

While those make their way around, let’s do a quick recap. We have been talking a lot about tiny electronic switches, otherwise known as transistors. Back in the 1950s, the first semiconductor-based transistors were pretty bulky and, frankly, a bit crude. But over the decades, the engineering has become incredibly sophisticated.

We went from squeezing a single transistor onto a chip to packing in thousands, then millions, and now we are looking at state-of-the-art chips with hundreds of billions of transistors. And they are not just laying them out flat anymore; once you run out of floor space, you start building skyscrapers. Engineers are stacking multiple layers of transistors on top of each other, though this gets technologically difficult because any microscopic roughness on one layer propagates and worsens on the next.

This relentless drive to pack more computational power into a given area is driven by what we call Moore’s Law. I can almost guarantee this will show up on your next quiz!

Remember, Moore’s Law is not a law of physics; it is a law of the market. Companies have to keep innovating to maintain a competitive advantage. If you stand still, you go out of business. The result is that the number of transistors on a chip has doubled roughly every two years. Over the past 50 years, that is about 25 doubling cycles. If you do the math, two raised to the power of 25 is about 30 million. That is a 30-million-fold increase in transistor density over half a century. It is an astonishing engineering achievement.

The Diffraction Limit: When Light Misbehaves

So, what physically limits this process? What determines how small we can make these transistor features? It all comes down to the tool we use for patterning: photolithography. Photolithography relies on light, and light is an electromagnetic wave.

Different colors of light have different wavelengths. Blue light sits around 450 nanometers, while red light is up in the 600 to 700 nanometer range. If you want to make smaller patterns, you need a smaller wavelength, which is why we move into the ultraviolet (UV) spectrum.

You might naively think that the wavelength does not matter—that as long as you make a tiny slit in your mask, you can shine any light through it and get a tiny pattern. Unfortunately, physics gets in the way. This brings us to the diffraction limit.

When you pass light through a slit that is much larger than its wavelength, it behaves exactly as you would expect: it travels straight through. But when you get greedy and try to squeeze that light through a slit that is smaller than its wavelength, the light stops traveling in a straight line. It bends and spreads out in all directions. Because of this spreading, you cannot pattern a feature that is significantly smaller than the wavelength of the light you are using.

This gives us a very practical rule of thumb: the smallest feature you can pattern is roughly equal to the wavelength of the light. In our cleanroom here at Virginia Tech, we use UV light with a wavelength of 365 nanometers. Industry giants like Intel and TSMC use Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography, which operates at a tiny 13.5 nanometer wavelength, allowing them to carve out those incredibly small, state-of-the-art transistors.

Seeing the Unseeable: The Limits of Microscopy

This same rule of waves applies not just to making things, but to seeing things. If you want to resolve an object clearly, you need to probe it with a wave whose wavelength is comparable to, or smaller than, the object itself.

Imagine trying to measure the exact shape of a pebble by throwing massive ocean swells at it—the waves would just wash right over it without giving you any detail. You need tiny ripples to detect the tiny pebble.

A standard optical microscope uses visible light, which means it is great for looking at things on the micron scale, like red blood cells (which are about 10 to 20 microns across). You can even buy UV microscopes to see smaller things like viruses. But if you want to see a single atom, which is a fraction of a nanometer wide, visible and UV light simply will not cut it. The wavelengths are dozens of times too big.

Accuracy Note

Possible error: Human red blood cells have a diameter of roughly 6–8 micrometers, not 10–20 microns; the stated range is roughly double the actual size.

Correction: Red blood cells are typically about 6–8 micrometers in diameter.

So, why not just use electromagnetic waves with even shorter wavelengths?

Someone in class asked a great question: why not use gamma rays or X-rays? In principle, X-rays have wavelengths down around 0.1 nanometers (1 Angstrom), which is exactly the scale of an atom. The problem is an engineering one. We know how to make glass lenses to focus visible light. Making lenses that can effectively focus X-rays is incredibly difficult. Furthermore, generating a stable, high-intensity X-ray source is a massive, expensive undertaking. So while there is no strict physical law preventing an X-ray microscope, the technological barriers make it highly impractical for routine nanoscale imaging.

Enter the Electron: Wave-Particle Duality

If X-rays are too hard to wrangle, what is our alternative? We use electrons.

Now, I know what you are thinking. You have been taught that an electron is a particle—a tiny little sphere of negative charge orbiting a nucleus. But welcome to the bizarre world of quantum mechanics! Under the right conditions, an electron can behave like a wave.

This concept is known as wave-particle duality. Because electrons can act as waves, we can use them for microscopy (seeing things) and lithography (patterning things). You have likely heard of Scanning Electron Microscopes (SEM) or Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEM). These instruments rely entirely on the wave-like nature of the electron to achieve incredible nanoscale resolution.

The de Broglie Wavelength

To figure out exactly how small of a wave an electron produces, we use a concept named after a French physicist, Louis de Broglie. (Pro tip: it looks like it should be pronounced "de Brog-lee," but it is actually pronounced "de Broy," kind of like "bro").

The de Broglie wavelength formula is beautifully simple. It connects a wave property (wavelength) directly to a particle property (momentum). The equation is:

\begin{equation} \lambda = \frac{h}{p} \tag{1} \end{equation}

Here, \lambda (the Greek letter lambda) is the wavelength. On the top of the fraction, h is Planck’s constant, a fundamental number in physics equal to roughly 6.63 \times 10^{-34} Joules times seconds. On the bottom, p is the momentum of the electron.

If you recall from basic physics, momentum is just an object’s mass multiplied by its velocity (p = mv). So, we can rewrite the equation as:

\begin{equation} \lambda = \frac{h}{mv} \tag{2} \end{equation}

What does this mean for us in the lab? The mass of an electron (m) is fixed, and Planck’s constant (h) is, well, constant. The only thing we can change is the velocity (v). If we want a shorter wavelength to see smaller things, we need to increase the velocity of the electron.

When you are shopping for a high-end electron microscope, one of the main specs you look at is the accelerating voltage. A higher accelerating voltage pumps more kinetic energy into the electrons, making them move faster. Faster electrons mean a higher momentum, which results in a shorter de Broglie wavelength, ultimately giving you sharper images and the ability to resolve smaller features.

Of course, wavelength is not the only factor. To get a crisp image of an atom, you also need excellent "electron optics." Since we cannot use glass lenses for electrons, we use electromagnets. By running fast electrons through a carefully tuned magnetic field, we can bend their path and focus the beam. Combine that with highly sensitive detectors, and you have a machine capable of seeing the atomic building blocks of the universe.

Back-of-the-Envelope Quantum Mechanics

Let’s put some numbers to this and do a quick back-of-the-envelope calculation. Suppose we accelerate an electron to 5% of the speed of light. What would its de Broglie wavelength be? We will round our numbers to make the math easy to do without a calculator.

First, let’s gather our variables:

  • Planck’s constant (h): The actual value is 6.63 \times 10^{-34} J\cdots. Let’s round 6.63 up to 10. That changes our order of magnitude, giving us h \approx 10 \times 10^{-34} = 10^{-33} J\cdots.

  • Mass of an electron (m): The actual value is 9.1 \times 10^{-31} kg. Let’s round 9.1 up to 10, giving us m \approx 10 \times 10^{-31} = 10^{-30} kg.

  • Velocity (v): The speed of light (c) is 3 \times 10^8 m/s. We want 5% of that, which is 0.05 \times (3 \times 10^8) = 0.15 \times 10^8 m/s. Let’s round 0.15 down to 0.1. This gives us v \approx 0.1 \times 10^8 = 10^7 m/s.

Now, let’s plug these rounded values into our de Broglie equation:

\begin{align*} \lambda &= \frac{h}{mv} \\ \lambda &\approx \frac{10^{-33} \text{ J}\cdot\text{s}}{(10^{-30} \text{ kg}) \times (10^7 \text{ m/s})} \\ \lambda &\approx \frac{10^{-33}}{10^{-23}} \frac{\text{J}\cdot\text{s}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}} \\ \lambda &\approx 10^{-10} \text{ m} \end{align*}

Let’s do a quick sanity check on those units to make sure we actually end up with a length. A Joule (J) is a unit of energy, which breaks down into \text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2 / \text{s}^2. If we substitute that into our unit fraction:

\begin{align*} \frac{\text{J}\cdot\text{s}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}} &= \frac{(\text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2 / \text{s}^2) \cdot \text{s}}{\text{kg} \cdot \text{m} / \text{s}} \\ &= \frac{\text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2 / \text{s}}{\text{kg} \cdot \text{m} / \text{s}} \\ &= \text{m} \end{align*}

The units cancel out exactly to meters, which is what we want for a wavelength!

So, our estimated wavelength is 10^{-10} meters. This is equal to 0.1 nanometers, or 1 Angstrom. This is right on the scale of individual atoms. By accelerating an electron to just a fraction of the speed of light, we generate a wave small enough to image the atomic realm.

Food for Thought: The Fastball Wave

I want to leave you with a thought experiment to discuss with your groups.

We just established that an electron behaves like both a particle and a wave. We also know that everyday objects, like a baseball, are made entirely of electrons, protons, and neutrons—all subatomic particles that physicists tell us exhibit wave-particle duality.

So, consider Jacob "The Miz" Misiorowski, a pitcher who can throw a baseball at 100 miles per hour. That baseball has mass, and it certainly has velocity, which means it has momentum. According to the de Broglie equation, anything with momentum has a wavelength.

Why, then, does a 100 mph fastball not behave like a wave? Why doesn’t it diffract around the batter’s bat? Talk it over with your group, write down your thoughts, and turn them in before you leave. We will dive into the answer next time!
